source_cards.front: What must you do when passing a stopped emergency vehicle?
source_cards.back: For a stopped emergency vehicle, slow to at least ten miles per hour below the posted limit and move over a lane if you safely can; if not, slow down and leave as much room as possible.

source_cards.front: What is the penalty for breaking the move-over law near emergency vehicles?
source_cards.back: Breaking the move-over law for authorized emergency vehicles is a civil infraction, rising to a felony if emergency personnel are injured or killed.

source_cards.front: How does your response differ for a stopped and an approaching emergency vehicle?
source_cards.back: For a stopped emergency vehicle you slow and move over, but for one approaching with lights and siren you pull to the edge and stop.

source_cards.front: How does the move-over penalty differ for police and for utility trucks?
source_cards.back: Violating the move-over law near police, fire or ambulance vehicles is a civil infraction, but near utility or garbage trucks it is a misdemeanor.

source_cards.front: How do the following distance for an emergency vehicle and the stopping distance for a school bus differ?
source_cards.back: Follow a moving emergency vehicle no closer than five hundred feet, yet stop at least twenty feet back from a school bus with flashing red lights.

needs.title: Crosswalks and stop positions

source_cards.front: How do you handle a stop sign or flashing red signal, and where do you stop?
source_cards.back: At a stop sign or flashing red signal, stop completely and check traffic, using the stop line or crosswalk, or else a spot where you can see approaching traffic without entering the intersection.

source_cards.front: Must you yield to a pedestrian in a marked crosswalk when your light is green?
source_cards.back: Yield to pedestrians in a marked crosswalk, whether at an intersection or midblock, even when your light is green.

source_cards.front: Which other pedestrians must you yield to?
source_cards.back: Yield to children in or near a school zone crosswalk while school is in session, and to pedestrians with physical, hearing or visual disabilities.

source_cards.front: Where no traffic control devices exist, when does a pedestrian in an unmarked crosswalk get the right of way?
source_cards.back: Where no traffic control devices exist, a pedestrian using an unmarked crosswalk on the driver's half of the road gets the right of way.

source_cards.front: Which other pedestrians must you yield to, even after the signal changes?
source_cards.back: Yield to a pedestrian who stepped into a crosswalk before the signal changed, and to one crossing from an alley, driveway, building or private road.

source_cards.front: Does a green light override a pedestrian already in the crosswalk?
source_cards.back: A green light never overrides a pedestrian already in the crosswalk.

source_cards.front: Which stopped vehicles and zones ban passing?
source_cards.back: Do not pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk or intersection for a pedestrian, in a posted no-passing construction zone, or when a school bus has stopped with red lights flashing.

needs.title: Intersections and right-of-way

source_cards.front: What does a green light not give you the right of way over?
source_cards.back: A green light does not give you the right of way over vehicles still clearing the intersection or over oncoming traffic when you turn left.

source_cards.front: Who goes first at a four-way stop, and who yields on a tie?
source_cards.back: At a four-way stop, the first driver to arrive and stop goes first, and when two arrive together the vehicle on the left yields to the one on its right.

source_cards.front: At a T-intersection with no signs or signals, who has the right of way?
source_cards.back: At a T-intersection with no signals or signs, vehicles on the through road have the right of way.

source_cards.front: At a four-way stop, when does the left driver yield to the right?
source_cards.back: At a four-way stop the first to stop goes first, and only on a tie does the driver on the left yield to the driver on the right.

source_cards.front: What right of way does a funeral procession have?
source_cards.back: A funeral procession has the right of way over all vehicles except fire trucks, ambulances and police vehicles.

source_cards.front: Where no traffic control devices exist, when does a pedestrian in an unmarked crosswalk get the right of way?
source_cards.back: Where no traffic control devices exist, a pedestrian using an unmarked crosswalk on the driver's half of the road gets the right of way.

needs.title: Passing and no-passing situations

source_cards.front: Who should you be ready to yield to in work areas and near stopped service vehicles?
source_cards.back: Be ready to yield to workers in construction or maintenance areas and when nearing or passing a stopped garbage, utility or road maintenance vehicle with flashing lights.

source_cards.front: When may you pass on a two-lane highway?
source_cards.back: On a two-lane highway, pass only with a clear view of the left lane and oncoming traffic far enough away to give you the time and distance to pass safely.

source_cards.front: After passing, when may you move back to the right?
source_cards.back: After passing, do not cut back right until the whole vehicle you passed shows in your rearview mirror.

source_cards.front: What extra care applies when towing, passing several vehicles or following a passer?
source_cards.back: Allow extra passing room when towing a trailer, pass only one vehicle at a time, and do not tailgate a vehicle that is passing slower traffic.

source_cards.front: What care is needed when passing in a three-lane road's center lane?
source_cards.back: Use extreme care when passing in the center lane of a three-lane road, since oncoming drivers may enter it too, and never use it to pass or merge when it is marked for left turns only.

source_cards.front: When may you pass on the right?
source_cards.back: You may pass on the right on a two-lane road with room when the vehicle ahead is turning left, on a multi-lane one-way street, on roads with two or more lanes each way, or where the road is widened for passing.

source_cards.front: When do lane markings, signs, hills or curves ban passing?
source_cards.back: Passing is banned when your side of the center has a solid yellow line, when no-passing signs are posted, or when a hill or curve hides oncoming traffic.

source_cards.front: What traffic, view or lane conditions ban passing?
source_cards.back: Do not pass when oncoming traffic is too close, when you cannot see clearly ahead, or when the three-lane center lane is marked left turn only.

source_cards.front: Which stopped vehicles and zones ban passing?
source_cards.back: Do not pass a vehicle stopped at a crosswalk or intersection for a pedestrian, in a posted no-passing construction zone, or when a school bus has stopped with red lights flashing.

source_cards.front: How do the two hundred foot and one hundred foot passing distances differ?
source_cards.back: After passing, you must be back in your lane before you are within two hundred feet of oncoming traffic, while the no-passing distance near intersections and railroad crossings is one hundred feet.

source_cards.back: You must yield to other vehicles when turning right, including a right turn at a red light.

source_cards.front: When may you turn left on a green light, and what if it turns red mid-turn?

source_cards.front: What does a green light not give you the right of way over?

source_cards.back: Merge signs near entrances warn of entering traffic; adjust speed or change lanes safely to help them merge, and watch for drivers who brake or swerve suddenly toward an exit.

source_cards.front: Under Michigan's merge law, who must yield and adjust?
source_cards.back: Michigan's merge law, MCL two hundred fifty-seven point six four nine(seven), means the merging driver must yield to traffic close enough to be an immediate hazard and adjust speed and position to merge safely, whether entering or leaving the freeway.

source_cards.front: When merging onto a freeway, who adjusts speed and position?
source_cards.back: The merging driver, not freeway traffic, must adjust speed and placement to merge safely.

source_cards.front: How do you steer out of a skid?
source_cards.back: In a skid, lift off the accelerator, point the front wheels only where you want to go, expect a secondary skid the other way, steer again, then straighten the wheels.

source_cards.front: What is hydroplaning, and what makes it more likely?
source_cards.back: Hydroplaning happens when tires ride on top of water and can cost you control; worn tires, low pressure and too much speed make it more likely.

needs.title: Vehicle blind spots

source_cards.front: Where are a car's blind spots, and how should the inside mirror be set?
source_cards.back: Most cars have at least two blind spots, to the left rear and right rear, that side mirrors cannot show; set the inside mirror to show the center of the road behind you.

source_cards.front: How should you set the outside mirrors?
source_cards.back: Set the outside mirrors so the vehicle's edges just show from a normal seating position, or for fewer blind spots lean left to the window to set the left mirror and lean right to the center to set the right one.

needs.title: Following and stopping distance

source_cards.front: What factors affect your stopping distance?
source_cards.back: Stopping distance depends on fatigue, attention, the vehicle's type and weight, tire and brake condition, road surface and weather.

source_cards.front: What following distance is required on dry or wet pavement?
source_cards.back: On dry or wet pavement, a following distance of three to four seconds is required.

source_cards.front: How do you check your following distance?
source_cards.back: To check following distance, count one-thousand-one through one-thousand-three from when the vehicle ahead passes a fixed point; reaching that point before you finish counting three seconds means you are too close.

source_cards.front: When should you stretch your following distance, and to how much?
source_cards.back: At higher speeds or in adverse conditions, stretch your following distance to six seconds or more if needed.

source_cards.front: How should you use your eyes, and when should you add following distance?
source_cards.back: Avoid staring at any one thing for more than a few seconds, and increase following distance at night, in bad weather, at rush hour, during lane changes and near intersections.

source_cards.front: How do following time and look-ahead time differ?
source_cards.back: Following distance starts at three to four seconds and may rise to six seconds or more, while looking ahead means scanning twenty to thirty seconds down the road.
